reference: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2021). Standard polysomnography: AAST technical guideline. https://www.aastweb.org/Portals/0/Docs/Resources/Guidelines/AAST%20PSG%20Guideline%20Final.pdf · Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Elsevier.

stations.title: Protect the patient and assess urgency first

study.intro: A troubleshooting sequence starts by deciding whether the problem is technical, physiologic, or potentially urgent.
points: Look at and assess the patient when the tracing suggests a possible acute problem rather than assuming artifact.
Use video, audio, direct observation, symptoms, and neighboring physiologic channels to establish context.
If there is an immediate safety concern, follow the active emergency procedure and chain of command before pursuing routine signal correction.
Do not let a technically unusual waveform distract from the patient’s actual condition.

apply.prompt: A new abnormal ECG pattern appears while the patient reports chest discomfort and looks distressed. What should the technologist do first?
options: Assess the patient immediately and follow the facility emergency/escalation procedure
Change the ECG sensitivity until the tracing looks normal
Disconnect and reconnect every sensor before checking the patient
Wait several minutes to see whether the pattern disappears
apply.answer: Assess the patient immediately and follow the facility emergency/escalation procedure
apply.hint: Separate a possible patient emergency from a routine technical problem before touching display settings.
apply.rationale: Patient assessment and the facility safety pathway come before ordinary artifact troubleshooting when symptoms or clinical distress suggest urgency.

recap.canDo: Distinguish a routine technical correction from a situation that requires immediate assessment and escalation.

stations.title: Define the problem and affected data

visual.label: Onset + distribution + behavior narrow the cause

study.intro: Before changing equipment, describe exactly what changed and where.
points: Identify the onset time and whether the change was abrupt or gradual.
List the affected channels and compare them with channels that remain clean.
Decide whether the problem is continuous, intermittent, position-linked, movement-linked, or event-linked.
Use the distribution of affected data to decide whether to investigate one sensor, a shared pathway, or the acquisition system.

apply.prompt: At 02:13, EEG, EOG, chin EMG, ECG, airflow, effort, and oximetry all become flat at nearly the same moment. Which observation is most useful before reapplying individual sensors?
options: The simultaneous multi-system onset suggests a common acquisition or connection problem
Every individual sensor probably failed independently at the same second
Only the EEG channels need to be inspected
The event can be ignored because several channels changed together
apply.answer: The simultaneous multi-system onset suggests a common acquisition or connection problem
apply.hint: Ask what single failure could affect many unrelated channel types at the same time.
apply.rationale: A common abrupt onset across unrelated systems should push troubleshooting toward a shared connection, headbox, amplifier, acquisition, power, or display pathway before multiple independent sensor failures are assumed.

recap.reviewed: How timing and channel distribution localize a problem before intervention.
recap.canDo: Describe a signal problem precisely enough to choose the next troubleshooting branch.

stations.title: Localize the source through the signal pathway

visual.label: Trace from patient context through the recording chain

study.intro: Troubleshoot systematically through the recording pathway instead of changing several variables at once.
points: Trace the likely path from patient/signal source to sensor or electrode, lead/connector, headbox or input, amplifier/acquisition system, and display/storage.
When several derivations share one reference or input, compare them with derivations that use a different reference.
A disturbance limited to channels sharing one electrode or reference is evidence for a shared-pathway problem.
Secure connections and verify sensor/electrode integrity before using display filters as a shortcut for unexplained artifact.

apply.prompt: F3-M2, C3-M2, E1-M2, and E2-M2 become noisy together, while F4-M1, C4-M1, chin EMG, and ECG remain comparatively clean. What should be inspected first?
options: The shared M2 reference pathway
The chin EMG electrodes
The ECG derivation
Every channel independently
apply.hint: Group the affected derivations by what they have in common.
apply.rationale: The affected channels share M2, while channels using M1 or separate bipolar derivations remain comparatively clean. That pattern localizes the first check to the shared M2 pathway.

recap.reviewed: Systematic signal-pathway tracing and shared-reference localization.
recap.canDo: Use affected-versus-clean channel patterns to identify the most likely shared source.

stations.title: Correlate physiology, video, and neighboring channels

visual.label: One channel rarely tells the whole story

study.intro: Artifact recognition improves when the suspicious signal is compared with independent evidence.
points: Compare the suspicious channel with physiologically related channels and with signals that should not share the same source.
Use synchronized video, body position, movement, snoring/audio, and technologist observations when available.
Ask whether the morphology and timing are physiologically plausible before calling a pattern true physiology.
A channel that changes with movement or cable tension may require a different correction than a true physiologic event.

apply.prompt: Large transient deflections appear in several channels exactly when video shows the patient turning, then disappear when movement stops. What is the best next interpretation step?
options: Correlate the movement, neighboring channels, and signal recovery before labeling the deflections as physiology
Score the deflections as a physiologic event based on amplitude alone
Turn on additional filtering before checking video
Delete the affected segment from the recording
apply.answer: Correlate the movement, neighboring channels, and signal recovery before labeling the deflections as physiology
apply.hint: Use evidence that is independent of the suspicious waveform.
apply.rationale: Synchronized behavior and cross-channel timing help separate patient-generated movement artifact from true physiology and protect both scoring and later interpretation.

recap.reviewed: Cross-channel and video correlation before labeling artifact or physiology.
recap.canDo: Use independent context to test whether a suspicious waveform is believable.

stations.title: Apply the least disruptive correction and recheck

visual.label: One targeted correction → verify the result

study.intro: A correction is not complete until the technologist confirms that it solved the problem without creating a new one.
points: Choose the most likely cause and change one variable when practical so the effect is interpretable.
Prefer the least disruptive correction that restores valid data while protecting patient comfort and sleep continuity.
After any sensor, lead, connection, montage, sensitivity, or other technical change, recheck the affected signal and related channels.
Do not use aggressive filtering as a first-line substitute for finding a correctable artifact source because filtering can distort physiologic data.

apply.prompt: Nasal pressure becomes weak after the patient changes position, while effort and thermal airflow remain credible. What is the best targeted first correction?
options: Inspect and reposition the nasal pressure interface, then verify the signal
Change filters on all respiratory channels
Replace every respiratory sensor at once
Leave the signal unchanged because other channels still work
apply.answer: Inspect and reposition the nasal pressure interface, then verify the signal
apply.hint: The problem is localized; choose the smallest intervention that tests the most likely cause.
apply.rationale: A localized post-position-change loss supports a targeted interface check followed by signal verification rather than broad changes that make the cause harder to identify.

recap.reviewed: Targeted correction, sleep preservation, and post-intervention verification.
recap.canDo: Correct one likely cause and prove that the recording improved afterward.

stations.title: Escalate unsafe, abnormal, or unresolved conditions

visual.label: Know when troubleshooting leaves the routine technical lane

study.intro: Some problems are not appropriate for bedside improvisation.
points: Escalate suspected emergencies, significant patient changes, electrical or equipment safety concerns, and unresolved problems according to facility policy.
Follow the active order, medical-director protocols, equipment instructions, and chain of command rather than inventing an unauthorized therapy or repair.
If equipment appears unsafe, remove it from patient use as required by facility procedure and use approved backup pathways when available.
Document who was contacted, why escalation occurred, and any resulting instruction or limitation.

apply.prompt: A bedside device develops an electrical odor and repeatedly faults during the recording. What is the best response?
options: Follow the facility equipment-safety procedure, remove the unsafe device from use as directed, and escalate for approved backup or service
Open the device and attempt an internal repair while it remains connected to the patient
Ignore the odor if the waveform is still visible
Increase display gain to compensate for the faults
apply.answer: Follow the facility equipment-safety procedure, remove the unsafe device from use as directed, and escalate for approved backup or service
apply.hint: This is an equipment safety problem, not a display-quality problem.
apply.rationale: Unsafe or malfunctioning equipment requires the facility safety/service pathway rather than improvised repair or continued patient use.

recap.reviewed: Escalation boundaries for patient safety, equipment safety, and unresolved technical problems.
recap.canDo: Recognize when the correct troubleshooting action is to stop, escalate, and use an approved alternative.

stations.title: Document the problem, action, response, and limitation

visual.label: Make the record reconstruct what happened

study.intro: Troubleshooting documentation protects later scoring, interpretation, quality review, and continuity of care.
points: Record when the problem began and ended and which channels or systems were affected.
Document the observation or likely cause, what intervention was performed, and the patient or signal response.
Record room entries, montage or setting changes, environmental disturbances, and unresolved data limitations when relevant.
A good handoff lets the scorer or interpreting clinician distinguish missing data, corrected artifact, true physiology, and residual uncertainty.

apply.prompt: Nasal pressure was unusable for 12 minutes, the cannula was repositioned, and a stable signal returned. Which note best protects study integrity?
options: Document onset/end time, affected signal, observed problem, cannula repositioning, restored signal quality, and any remaining limitation
Write only 'fixed sensor' with no time or channel
Do not document because the signal eventually returned
Document only the final stable signal and omit the lost interval
apply.answer: Document onset/end time, affected signal, observed problem, cannula repositioning, restored signal quality, and any remaining limitation
apply.hint: Could someone reviewing the study tomorrow reconstruct the data-quality gap and what was done about it?
apply.rationale: Timing, affected data, intervention, response, and residual limitation give later reviewers the context needed to judge study integrity.

recap.reviewed: Chronologic technical documentation and handoff after troubleshooting.
recap.canDo: Write a concise troubleshooting note that preserves the meaning and limitations of the recording.
